title: Kinematics

notes.heading: 1. Differential Kinematics, x-t / v-t Graphs & Uniform Acceleration
notes.proseLatex: Instantaneous velocity is $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$ (slope of $x$-$t$ graph) and acceleration is $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ (slope of $v$-$t$ graph). Signed area $\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ gives displacement $\Delta x$, while unsigned area $\int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v|\,dt$ gives total distance travelled. Under constant acceleration $a$, the three SUVAT equations plus $n$-th second displacement $s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$ hold strictly in vector form.

keyFormulas.label: Calculus Kinematics & n-th Second Displacement
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Connect x(t), v(t), a(x) via derivatives/integrals and compute nth-second displacement.

keyFormulas.label: Equal-Distance vs Equal-Time Average Speed
keyFormulas.latex: $v_{\text{avg, equal }d} = \frac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\;\text{(harmonic)},\qquad v_{\text{avg, equal }t} = \frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\;\text{(arithmetic)}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Avoid mixing up equal-distance harmonic mean with equal-time arithmetic mean.

examples.problemLatex: A car accelerates uniformly from rest for $4\text{ s}$ at $3\text{ m/s}^2$, then cruises at constant velocity for $6\text{ s}$. Find total displacement and describe the $x$-$t$ curve.
stepsLatex: Phase 1 ($0\le t\le 4$): $x_1 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(4^2) = 24\text{ m}$ (upward-concave parabola), reaching $v = 12\text{ m/s}$.
Phase 2 ($4\le t\le 10$): $x_2 = 12 \times 6 = 72\text{ m}$ (tangent straight line), so total displacement $= 96\text{ m}$.

notes.heading: 2. 2D Projectile Motion & Relative Velocity
notes.proseLatex: Launching at speed $u$ and angle $\theta$ above horizontal decouples into uniform horizontal motion ($v_x = u\cos\theta$) and vertical free fall ($a_y = -g$), giving parabolic path $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$. Complementary launch angles $\theta$ and $(90^\circ - \theta)$ yield identical horizontal range $R$ with height ratio $H_1/H_2 = \tan^2\theta$, and $R$ peaks at $\theta = 45^\circ$ ($R_{\max} = u^2/g$). Relative velocity is $\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$.

keyFormulas.label: Projectile Time of Flight, Max Height & Range
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Solve projectile range, height, and angle ratios without separate step derivations.

examples.problemLatex: At what projection angle $\theta$ does the horizontal range equal four times the maximum height ($R = 4H$)?

notes.heading: 3. Uniform & Non-Uniform Circular Kinematics
notes.proseLatex: For radius $r$, linear speed $v = \omega r$ is tangential while centripetal acceleration $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$ ALWAYS points radially inward even at constant speed ($\Delta\vec{v} \neq \vec{0}$!). When speed also changes, tangential acceleration $a_t = \frac{dv}{dt} = \alpha r$ combines orthogonally with $a_c$ to give net acceleration $a_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$.

keyFormulas.label: Centripetal & Total Acceleration in Circular Motion
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Separate radial direction-change acceleration from tangential speed-change acceleration.

wbjeebTraps: Signed area under $v$-$t$ gives DISPLACEMENT; flip negative lobes positive ($\int |v|\,dt$) when asked for TOTAL DISTANCE.
At the apex of projectile flight, vertical velocity $v_y = 0$, NOT total velocity: $v_{\text{top}} = u\cos\theta$ and $\vec{a} = -g\hat{j} \perp \vec{v}_{\text{top}}$.
In uniform circular motion, speed and kinetic energy are constant, yet velocity $\vec{v}$, momentum $\vec{p}$, and acceleration $\vec{a}_c$ are ALL continuously changing direction!
